transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor, it’s the bridges, really. I mean, I came because when I know I have to cross one—when there’s no other way around—my heart starts thumping before I’m even on it. My hands get damp on the steering wheel, or the armrest if someone else is driving, and this awful rush of fear just comes over me.

It’s funny, I used to drive all over years ago, back when roads were simpler—or maybe I was simpler, I don’t know. But now, if a bridge crossing is unavoidable, it starts right away. That’s what brought me in.
Is this fear limited to certain types of bridges, like very high or long ones, or does it happen with all bridges regardless of their size or height?

It’s mostly those high spans, doctor—the ones where I can see them coming up, or even if I see them on the map beforehand. I know, rationally, thousands of cars go over them every day without a thing happening. I tell myself that.

But when it’s there through the windshield, it feels like the whole bridge is just… waiting to drop away underneath us. It’s not sensible, I know. Smaller little bridges don’t always do that to me, but the high ones, the ones that rise up over water or traffic—those are the ones that get me. Funny, my father used to love driving scenic routes, always pointing out the engineering, but I never thought I’d end up afraid of something people built so carefully.
Do you find yourself avoiding other situations or places where you might feel trapped or overwhelmed, like tunnels, highways, or crowded spaces?

I’m not sure I’ve really noticed it with those other places in the same way. Tunnels, highways, crowds… I mean, highways can be unpleasant just because people drive like they’re late to their own wedding, you know, but I don’t know that it’s the same thing.

Crowded spaces, well, at my age I don’t go looking for crowds much anyway. I used to go to ball games with a friend from college—he always insisted on keeping score by hand, very old-fashioned—but that’s neither here nor there. I suppose what I know for sure is the bridges are what stand out to me. The rest… I’d have to think about it.
Have you ever had sudden, intense episodes of fear or discomfort that peaked within minutes, not just on bridges but in other places as well?

I’m not sure, doctor. I mean, I know what happens with the bridges, but in other places… I can’t say I’ve really kept track of something like that.

There have been times I’ve felt suddenly uneasy, I suppose, but whether it “peaked within minutes,” as you put it—well, I wouldn’t know how to measure that. My wife used to say I noticed every little noise in a restaurant but couldn’t remember where I put my glasses, so maybe I’m not the best reporter of myself.

What I know clearly is the bridge situation. Outside of that, I’d have to think on it more.
Can you think of a time when you felt a sudden rush of fear or discomfort that came on quickly, maybe with a racing heart or trouble breathing, even when you weren’t near a bridge?

I’m trying to think of one, doctor… and nothing comes to mind clearly like that. Not away from a bridge, anyway.

I mean, I’ve had moments where I get startled or uncomfortable—everybody does, I suppose. The telephone ringing late at night used to do that to me, back when my mother was still living, because you always assumed bad news at that hour. Funny how that sticks with you. But that’s not quite what you’re asking, is it?

A sudden rush with the heart and breathing and all that when I’m nowhere near a bridge… I can’t really give you a solid example. The bridge thing is the one I can point to. Everything else gets a bit fuzzy when I try to pin it down.
Have you ever experienced a sudden wave of fear or panic that came out of the blue, even when there wasn’t a bridge or anything specific scaring you?

I don’t think so… not that I can really put my finger on. If there wasn’t a bridge, or something clear like that, I can’t say I’ve had it just come out of nowhere.

Now, I do get nervous about things sometimes—who doesn’t, at 87? The mail comes late and you wonder if they lost something important, or the kettle makes a funny noise and suddenly you’re thinking of the time my neighbor’s stove went bad. But that’s more ordinary worry, I suppose.

A sudden wave of panic for no reason… I’m not sure I’ve noticed that. The bridge is the thing that makes sense to me when I think about it.

Have you ever had a panic attack—where you suddenly felt intense fear, maybe with a racing heart, sweating, or feeling like you couldn’t breathe—when you weren’t on or near a bridge, and there wasn’t an obvious reason for it?

No, I don’t think so, doctor. Not when I’m away from a bridge and nothing’s happening.

I’ve had plenty of ordinary frights, you know—someone knocking too hard at the door, or the television suddenly getting loud because I sat on the remote, silly things like that. But that’s not the same thing, I don’t think.

What you’re describing, the sudden panic with no reason behind it… I can’t say I’ve had that. At least not that I remember. The bridge is the thing I know about.
Are there other places or situations you actively avoid because you're worried about feeling panicked or overwhelmed, even if you're not on a bridge?

I’m not sure I can name another place like that, doctor. Bridges are the one that stand out to me.

I mean, I don’t much care for crowded parking lots, but that’s mostly because people drive like they’ve forgotten which side is forward. My son says I complain about that every time, and he’s probably right. And big stores can be tiring, all those lights and carts rattling around… but I don’t think I avoid them because I’m afraid I’ll panic.

So no, not really. Not that I’ve noticed. The bridge is the thing I keep coming back to.
Have you ever had a sudden, intense episode of fear with symptoms like a racing heart, sweating, or trouble breathing, even if it wasn’t on a bridge and you didn’t go out of your way to avoid it?

I don’t believe so… not the way you’re describing it. I mean, I’ve had moments where I get startled or worked up, but that’s usually because something happened, you know?

My daughter used to say I’d jump if a book fell off a shelf, and she wasn’t wrong. I had this old bookcase that leaned a bit—should’ve fixed it years ago, but you put things off and then suddenly you’re 87 and everything in the house has a story attached to it.

But a sudden strong fear like that, with no bridge and no clear reason… I can’t really say I’ve had that. At least nothing that comes to mind.
Have you ever felt intense fear or panic in open spaces, like parking lots, markets, or while walking down a street, even when there wasn’t a bridge involved?

Open spaces… no, I don’t think that’s been a problem in that way.

Parking lots can make me grumble, sure, especially when someone leaves their cart right where you’re trying to pull in. I used to tell my wife that people should need a license just to handle those carts, and she’d laugh at me. Markets too, they can be noisy, but I wouldn’t say I feel panic there.

Walking down the street… no, not unless there’s something else going on. I don’t think open spaces by themselves do that to me.
Have you ever felt a sudden rush of fear or panic in enclosed spaces like tunnels, elevators, or on public transportation, even if you weren’t near a bridge?

I don’t think so… enclosed spaces, no, I can’t say that rings a bell.

I’ve been in elevators plenty, though I do sometimes think they don’t make them like they used to. The one at my old dentist’s office made a noise like a washing machine full of shoes—terrible thing. But I wouldn’t say I panicked in it.

Tunnels… I don’t go through many these days. Public transportation, not much anymore either. When I was younger I took buses now and then, and there was always someone talking too loud or coughing into the air like the whole bus needed to share it, but that’s more irritation than fear.

So, no… not that I’ve noticed. Not away from the bridge.
Have you ever felt a sudden rush of intense fear or panic in social situations, like speaking in front of people or being the center of attention?

Social situations… hmm. I don’t think I’d call it panic, no.

I never liked being fussed over, if that’s what you mean. Birthdays where everyone turns and sings at you—always felt a bit silly to me. My wife used to insist on making a cake, and I’d tell her, “At my age, the candles are a fire hazard,” though back then I wasn’t even all that old.

Speaking in front of people… I gave a toast once at my brother’s anniversary, and I was nervous, sure, but I think anyone would be. I don’t remember a sudden rush of fear or anything like that just from people looking at me. So… no, not really.
Have you ever had a sudden rush of fear or panic in enclosed spaces like tunnels, elevators, or on public transportation, even if you weren’t near a bridge?

I think you asked me that a moment ago, didn’t you? Enclosed spaces… no, I don’t really have that, not that I can tell.

Elevators don’t bother me beyond the usual annoyance when they stop at every floor. And buses—well, I haven’t been on one in ages, but I remember more about the smell of diesel and people talking too loud than any kind of panic.

So, no… if you mean a sudden rush of fear just because it’s enclosed, I haven’t noticed that.
Have you ever had a sudden rush of fear or panic when you were in a social situation or somewhere open like a parking lot, even if you weren’t near a bridge?

Social situations or parking lots… no, I don’t think so. Not a sudden rush of fear, anyway.

Parking lots can be a nuisance, mind you. People drive through them like they’re late for their own funeral, and half the time they don’t look where they’re backing up. I’ve always said they should make the painted lines brighter—especially after rain, you can’t see a thing.

But fear? Panic? No… I don’t recall feeling that just from being out in the open or around people. Not unless there’s something else going on.

Have you ever had a sudden rush of fear or panic that occurred in a completely open space, like a field or a large empty parking lot, where there was no bridge or anything else that you felt trapped by?

A completely open space… no, I can’t say I’ve had that, at least not that I remember.

Fields mostly make me think of when I was a boy—my uncle had this bit of land, and we’d be out there getting burrs stuck in our socks. Funny the things you remember. Large empty parking lots, well, they feel a little bleak sometimes, especially outside those big stores, but not frightening in the way you’re asking.

So… no sudden panic just because it’s open, no.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a specific phobia related to high bridges, characterized by marked fear and physiological arousal when encountering or anticipating such bridges. There is no evidence of panic attacks in other contexts or generalized anxiety, and the fear is restricted to this specific stimulus. This corresponds to other specified phobia (F40.29), as it does not fully meet criteria for more specific phobic subtypes like acrophobia or claustrophobia.
